summary: Defense innovation money is moving from prototypes into first production contracts: the first ever US laser weapon production deal ($464.8 million to AeroVironment), the first drone wingman jets (General Atomics and Anduril), and up to $3.2 billion for space based interceptor prototypes. Cheap mass, meaning drones and the systems that kill drones, gets the fastest growing budgets. Many of the best positioned builders (Anduril, Castelion, Epirus, General Atomics) are private, so public exposure comes through primes, parts makers and a few volatile small caps.

innovations.name: Counter drone and directed energy
innovations.what: Systems that detect and destroy small drones using radar, jammers, cheap interceptor missiles, lasers and high power microwaves.
innovations.stage_why: The Army signed its first ever production contract for a laser weapon in September 2026 and is nearly doubling small counter drone spending, but fielded numbers are still small next to the threat.

evidence.cost: Laser and microwave shots cost little per engagement versus missiles; Coyote interceptors were bought at about $125,000 each (600 for $75 million). Exact laser cost per shot unverified.
evidence.money: Army FY2027 request is $994 million for small counter drone systems, up from $596 million enacted in FY2026. JIATF-401 committed over $600 million for drone defenses. Epirus won $66.1 million for four Leonidas microwave prototypes and $43.55 million for Gen II. The Army plans at least 6,000 Coyote kinetic interceptors over FY2025 to FY2029.
evidence.revenue: AeroVironment won $464.8 million for the Enduring High Energy Laser (LOCUST X3, 30 kW) in September 2026. DroneShield 1H 2026 revenue was A$125.8 million, up 74%, with FY2026 guided A$250 to 270 million. Ondas raised its 2026 revenue target to at least $525 million after buying DZYNE.

spreads_to.use: Protecting airports, power plants, prisons and data centers from drones.
Guarding oil and gas sites, which drones have hit in recent wars.

innovations.bottleneck: High power laser sources and beam control, plus radar and RF detection that can find small drones. Production capacity at a few firms (AeroVironment BlueHalo unit, Epirus, RTX) limits how fast systems field.

next_milestone.event: FY2027 appropriations deciding the $994 million Army counter drone line; first E-HEL laser deliveries
next_milestone.timing: FY2027 budget late 2026 to early 2027; deliveries timing unverified

innovations.thesis_broken_if: Lasers fail in field use and the Army reverts to buying only missiles and guns.

innovations.name: Hypersonic strike and counter hypersonic defense
innovations.what: Missiles that fly above Mach 5 and maneuver, plus the interceptors and sensors meant to stop them.
innovations.stage_why: The first Army Dark Eagle battery only began fielding in early 2026 after years of slips, the Air Force HACM is still in development, and the Glide Phase Interceptor will not finish development until 2028. Startups promise cheap mass production but have not fielded yet.

evidence.cost: Castelion says Blackbeard is designed for industrial scale; the Navy is paying $90 million for 50 missiles (about $1.8 million each). Kratos built its Erinyes test vehicle in three years for under $15 million.
evidence.approvals: Army and Navy flew a common hypersonic missile on March 26, 2026; a second Dark Eagle battery is planned by Q4 FY2026.
evidence.money: Castelion raised a $1 billion Series C at a $13 billion valuation (August 2026). Northrop's Glide Phase Interceptor contract rose by $475 million to $1.31 billion (April 2026). Raytheon has $985 million for HACM plus a $407.6 million add on. Kratos holds a MACH-TB 2.0 test bed contract worth up to $1.45 billion over 5 years.
evidence.revenue: Mostly development money today, not production revenue. Lockheed's PAC-3 deal ceiling of $58.6 billion shows how big missile defense production gets once programs mature.

spreads_to.use: Hypersonic test flights use small launch vehicles such as Rocket Lab HASTE.
Heat resistant alloys, ceramics and carbon composites.
Long term high speed aircraft research (speculative).

innovations.bottleneck: Solid rocket motors and heat shield materials, plus test range time. Motors come mostly from L3Harris (Aerojet) and Northrop, with new entrants like Ursa Major and Anduril scaling.

next_milestone.event: Second Dark Eagle battery fielded; Castelion Blackbeard fielding
next_milestone.timing: Dark Eagle Q4 FY2026; Blackbeard target 2027

innovations.thesis_broken_if: FY2027 budgets cut hypersonic procurement back to test only quantities or Golden Dome funding stalls.

innovations.name: Autonomous and attritable drones
innovations.what: Drones cheap enough to lose in combat, from small one way attack drones to jet powered wingmen that fly beside fighter jets.
innovations.stage_why: Both ends moved into production in 2026: the Air Force put its first Collaborative Combat Aircraft into production in June, and the Drone Dominance program is ordering tens of thousands of small attack drones.

evidence.cost: Drone Dominance budgets about $1 billion for roughly 340,000 small drones over two years, about $3,000 per drone.
evidence.approvals: Air Force awarded CCA Increment 1 production to General Atomics (FQ-42A) and Anduril (FQ-44A) in June 2026, four months early.
evidence.money: FY2027 request has $996.5 million to start CCA production plus $150 million advance procurement; the Air Force has signaled 100 to 150 Increment 1 aircraft. Drone Dominance plans to order 60,000 drones after the Gauntlet II round (August 2026), with 19 firms advancing.
evidence.revenue: AeroVironment fiscal Q1 2027 revenue was a record $480.5 million, up 6%, with $683 million of bookings and a $1.5 billion funded backlog; fiscal 2027 guide $2.125 to $2.225 billion.

spreads_to.use: Police and fire drones using the same US made platforms.
Inspection and spraying drones from the same parts base.
Autonomy software reused for cargo drones.

innovations.bottleneck: Non Chinese drone parts: motors, magnets, batteries, cameras and radios. US rules now bar Chinese parts, and only a few US suppliers make them at volume. Jam resistant navigation is a second constraint.

next_milestone.event: Drone Dominance Phase 2 orders (about 60,000 drones); FY2027 CCA procurement funding

innovations.thesis_broken_if: Drone Dominance orders shrink or slip a year, or CCA buys are cut in FY2027 appropriations.

innovations.name: AI cybersecurity
innovations.what: Security software that uses AI agents to find and stop attacks automatically, and new tools to secure the AI agents companies are deploying.
innovations.stage_why: Security budgets are mass market, but AI driven security operations and AI agent protection are new line items. Only about 6% of companies report an advanced AI security strategy, while attackers already use AI agents.

evidence.money: Google closed its $32 billion all cash Wiz purchase on March 11, 2026. Palo Alto closed its about $25 billion CyberArk purchase on February 11, 2026. Gartner sees 2026 security spending of $244.2 billion, up 13.3%, and the market for securing AI near $4.8 billion in 2027.
evidence.revenue: CrowdStrike ARR was $5.84 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 25%, with record net new ARR of $333 million; Falcon Flex ARR passed $2.29 billion, up 101%.

spreads_to.use: AI driven defense of networks against state hackers who already use AI agents.
Protecting patient and payment data against faster automated ransomware.
Securing factories, grids and robots as they connect to AI.

innovations.bottleneck: Security telemetry data at scale (endpoint, cloud, identity) to train detection models. CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Palo Alto and Google hold the largest data sets, which favors platforms over point products.

next_milestone.event: CrowdStrike and Palo Alto results showing AI and identity ARR growth; Zscaler AI security suite uptake
next_milestone.timing: Late 2026 earnings (CrowdStrike Q3 FY2027 around early December)

innovations.thesis_broken_if: Platform ARR growth slows below 15% even as AI attacks rise, showing buyers are not adding AI security budget.

innovations.name: Space based missile defense (Golden Dome)
innovations.what: Satellites that track missiles from orbit and, for the first time, interceptors based in space that could hit missiles soon after launch.
innovations.stage_why: Tracking satellites are launching in batches, but space based interceptors are only prototype contracts due by 2028. Full funding depends on Congress, and a Space Force general warned in August 2026 there is no Golden Dome if funding falters.

evidence.cost: Golden Dome estimate is $185 billion (up from $175 billion), with initial capability by 2028 and full architecture in the mid 2030s.
evidence.money: Space Systems Command awarded up to $3.2 billion of space based interceptor prototype deals to 12 firms (announced April 24, 2026), including SpaceX, Anduril, Lockheed, Northrop and Raytheon. Reconciliation provided $24.7 billion as a down payment. SDA Tranche 3 tracking awards totaled $3.5 billion (Lockheed $1.1 billion, L3Harris $843 million, Rocket Lab $805 million, Northrop $784 million).
evidence.revenue: Development and satellite build revenue at primes and Rocket Lab; SDA Tranche 2 tracking launches start Q4 FY2026, including 18 L3Harris satellites.

spreads_to.use: Satellite bus, launch and optical link demand that also serves broadband constellations.
Laser and RF crosslinks developed for defense flow into commercial networks.
Infrared sensors reused for wildfire and weather monitoring.

innovations.bottleneck: Launch capacity, which SpaceX dominates, plus space qualified infrared sensors and propulsion. Congressional funding beyond reconciliation is the real gate.

next_milestone.event: FY2027 appropriations and second reconciliation bill deciding Golden Dome funding; SDA Tranche 2 tracking launches

innovations.thesis_broken_if: Congress funds Golden Dome only at the $400 million base level without reconciliation money.
